articles.title: Designing Domes in the Digital Age: From Concept to Preliminary Estimate
articles.summary: Despite being among architecture's oldest structural forms, domes continue to offer possibilities for creating large, column-free spaces and working with circular or free-form geometries beyond conventional rectangular building types. Their evolution has been closely tied to changes in materials, construction methods, and design tools. Today, digital platforms are adding another layer to this process, allowing some of the decisions traditionally developed later in a project to be explored much earlier.

articles.summary: There is no harder place to build than a high mountain, and none where a building feels more provisional. articles.title: TH+ house / ODDO architects
articles.summary: Woven into the dense urban fabric of Hanoi , TH+ House occupies an extremely constrained plot just 2.5 metres wide, accessible only through a network of narrow pedestrian alleys and surrounded by the city's characteristic informal vertical houses. In Hanoi's alley neighbourhoods, density is not only a physical condition but also a social one. Shared tea, small businesses, children playing in the street, and spontaneous encounters create a strong sense of community within an otherwise highly compressed environment. This social intensity became an important premise for the design of TH+ House.

Early Transforming Furniture: Richard Neutra's Camel Table
articles.summary: In the 1930s Richard Neutra , the Austrian architect who'd made his home in California, designed an early example of flexible-use furniture. Neutra conceived of a table that could transform from dining height to coffee table height, using a simple mechanism in the legs: Neutra made no secret of his inspiration for the design: He had it prototyped in 1940, and in 1951 designed a steel-leg version for a client. The table never went into mass production, but was occasionally produced for clients; occasionally these pop up on auction sites.

Their Marsh Model H machine, which rolled out in 1940, is still in use and sold today. Inside are case-hardened steel dies and zinc alloy punches designed to maintain crisp edges over time. articles.summary: You have to wonder what the pioneers of industrial design would make of this day and age. The original promise of ID was to harness the power of mass production to create useful objects for the masses. But now, in the second (or arguably third) century of ID as a field, we're awash in disposable junk, much of it plastic, none of it durable enough to be passed down to grandchildren. And there has been a reaction. So accustomed have we become to junk, that to design something durable is practically seen as subversive.
